extracted.intended_audience: businesses offering negative-option features, their legal and compliance counsel, industry trade groups, and regulators (FTC/State AGs)
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and compliance guidance for the FTC's final Rule governing negative option features (automatic renewals, free-to-pay conversions, continuity plans, etc.), including definitions, scope (including B2B), misrepresentations, and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seller responsibility when using third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Sellers must evaluate their commercial relationships with the Rule's provisions in mind and may satisfy obligations by contracting with third parties who act in accordance with the Rule and monitoring those parties' performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exemption for sellers who contract with third parties would nullify the Rule by incentivizing deceptive practices. A seller cannot evade its responsibility by contracting with a third party who does not act honestly with consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: No industry-wide exemption for insurance or state-regulated service contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission declines to exempt insurance or service contracts from the Rule; the final Rule is enforceable only against covered persons and activities within the Commission's jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The McCarran-Ferguson Act does not broadly bar FTC jurisdiction except where entities are subject to State regulation; activities beyond the 'business of insurance' remain subject to FTC. Existing State disclosures that already provide Rule protections should not burden sellers; however, state law does not create an industry-wide exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: B2B transactions are covered
rubrics_metrics.description: The final Rule covers business-to-business (B2B) transactions; section 5 of the FTC Act protects business consumers as well as individual consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rule preserves the ability of sophisticated business consumers to individually negotiate terms. The cancellation mechanism requirement (see separate criterion) incorporates a symmetrical standard to account for individually negotiated B2B agreements. The Rule will be enforced consistent with section 5 precedent and prior enforcement history shows deceptive negative-option practices occur in B2B contexts, especially affecting small businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'negative option feature'
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract provision under which the consumer's silence or failure to take affirmative action to reject a good or service or to cancel an agreement is interpreted by the negative option seller as acceptance or continuing acceptance of an offer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term includes, but is not limited to, automatic renewals, continuity plans, free-to-pay conversion or fee-to-pay conversions, and pre-notification negative option plans. This definition is consistent with the TSR and ROSCA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and treatment of 'clear and conspicuous' disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC imports its long-develop definition of 'clear and conspicuous' and modifies it in the final Rule; the District of Columbia requirement that disclosures be visually proximate to any request for consumer consent is incorporated into a separate consent section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition substantially overlaps with California and D.C. negative option laws; commenters questioned hyperlink reliance and clarity of wording. The Commission modifies the definition in the section-by-section analysis to enhance clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of 'save' limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission removes the proposed definition of 'save' and declines to adopt the NPRM's proposed limitation on saves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The saves provision did not strike the right balance between protecting consumers and allowing sellers to present useful subscription details prior to cancellation; the Commission may consider an SNPRM in the future. Without the 'save' limitation, sellers may present consumer-friendly details about a subscription before cancellation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of 'material' and 'interactive electronic medium' definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission adds definitions of 'material' and 'interactive electronic medium' to the Rule for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition of 'material' is adopted consistent with the TSR and section 5: material means likely to affect a person's choice of, or conduct regarding, goods or services. Other contested terms (e.g., 'simple cancellation mechanism', 'practical', 'normal business hours') are addressed via clarifying text rather than formal definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on misrepresenting 'any material fact'
rubrics_metrics.description: The final Rule prohibits misrepresentation of 'any material fact' (omitting the NPRM's broader phrasing referencing 'any material fact related to the transaction...or any material fact related to the underlying good or service').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To enhance clarity, the Rule defines 'material' consistent with section 5 and the TSR and provides a non-exhaustive list of potentially material fact categories. The prohibition is consistent with ROSCA and Commission precedent and allows the FTC to seek civil penalties where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-exclusive categories of potentially material facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule's text includes a non-exhaustive list of categories the Commission has identified as potentially material for more than 40 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples enumerated include cost, purpose or efficacy, and health or safety; the record also identifies characteristics of the seller, the format of the ad or sales communication, consumer authorization, consumer privacy or data security, and endorsements/testimonials. The list is non-exhaustive because dishonest actors may employ other material misrepresentations in the future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule scope includes misrepresentations beyond the negative option feature itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission declines to limit the misrepresentation prohibition solely to elements of the negative option feature and instead prohibits misrepresentation of any material facts connected to inducing consumers into negative option programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting the prohibition to the negative option element would be inconsistent with ROSCA and existing protections and could invite actors to misrepresent other transaction elements to evade liability. Sellers themselves have identified non-negative-option transaction elements (e.g., savings, convenience) as drivers of enrollment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: prevalence and consumer inability to police negative option misrepresentations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission's record and enforcement history demonstrate that misrepresentations to induce consumers into negative option programs are prevalent and often escape consumer self-policing because recurring charges can occur before consumers detect the misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because negative option transactions bypass typical re-evaluation steps required for repeat purchases, additional rule protections are warranted. The Rule targets the specific practice of misrepresenting material facts to induce consent to negative option features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement tools and remedies under the Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: As a trade regulation rule under section 18, the Rule defines deceptive acts/practices and includes requirements to prevent them; it provides for FTC enforcement (including civil penalties where appropriate) against covered conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rule clarifies prohibited conduct and enhances the Commission's ability to seek remedies (e.g., civil penalties) where existing section 5 or other rules do not already allow such relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation mechanism parity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule requires that the cancellation mechanism be 'at least as easy to use' as the consent mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This symmetrical standard accommodates individually negotiated B2B agreements by allowing negotiation of the cancellation mechanism alongside negotiation of consent to negative option terms. The cancellation mechanism provision pertains only to cancellation of the negative option feature and does not automatically terminate unrelated contract provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and specificity through definitions and examples rather than overly vague or broad language
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission revises proposed language to avoid vagueness and overbreadth (responding to commenters' concerns that the NPRM language was vague), by defining 'material' and listing examples and by addressing other contested terms through section-by-section clarification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The approach balances notice to regulated parties with coverage of the distinct deceptive practices the Rule targets; the Commission declined to adopt some narrow suggested limits (e.g., restricting misrepresentations to only negative option elements) and instead provides targeted definitions and examples to increase clarity.
